query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Minor additions of Al to high-entropy-alloy coatings (2–8 at.% in an otherwise fixed composition) increase local atomic ordering, leading to higher hardness and reduced wear rates under moderate to high contact loads and temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy coating (e.g., CoCrFeNi-based) deposited by magnetron sputtering without Al doping
generation.intervention: Incrementally introduce 2–8 at.% Al into the base coating composition while maintaining all other processing parameters (e.g., sputtering conditions, substrate preparation) constant
generation.conditions: Pin-on-disk wear tests at both room temperature and moderately elevated temperatures (e.g., up to 500°C), using identical load and sliding speed for each sample
generation.structural_mediator: Short-range atomic ordering promoted by Al, stabilizing local BCC or dual-phase microstructures and increasing dislocation barriers
generation.mechanism: The partial replacement by Al creates local ordering and lattice distortion that enhances hardness and impedes dislocation motion and abrasive damage, thereby reducing wear rates
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline (0% Al), coatings with 2–8 at.% Al will exhibit measurably higher hardness and lower wear rates. Friction coefficients may also trend lower for Al-doped coatings in the same testing conditions
generation.baseline: Baseline (0% Al) high-entropy-alloy coating tested under identical tribological and thermal conditions
generation.boundary: Beneficial effects are expected when Al doping remains in the specified 2–8 at.% range. Beyond this range, phase destabilization or excessive precipitation may degrade wear performance
generation.uncertainty: Exact improvement magnitude may vary depending on specific base alloy composition and testing temperatures. Wear or oxidation mechanisms may dominate at extremes of load and environment, limiting the effect

falsification_experiment.design: Deposit multiple coatings with Al doping increments (e.g., 0, 2, 8 at.%), test each under identical load/sliding speed at multiple temperatures via pin-on-disk tribometry, then measure hardness, friction coefficient, and volumetric wear loss
measurements: Microhardness before and after tribological testing
Coefficient of friction under consistent load/speed
Wear track depth and volume loss
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If systematic Al additions in the specified range do not significantly change hardness or reduce wear relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh-entropy alloy coatings (HEAC) exhibit good frictional wear and corrosion resistances, which are of importance for structure materials. In this study, the microstructure, surface morphology, hardness, frictional wear and corrosion resistance of an AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy coating synthesized by atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) were investigated. The frictional wear and corrosion resistance of the coating are simultaneously improved with an increase of the power of APS. The influence of the APS process on the microstructure and mechanical behavior is elucidated. The mechanisms of frictional wear and corrosion behavior of the AlCoCrFeNi HEAC are discussed in detail.Keywords: high-entropy alloy, coatings, atmospheric plasma spraying, frictional wear, corrosion

Treutler et al. [] found that Cr27.5Co14Fe22Mo22Ni11.65V2.8 shows the potential of generating a remelted wear- resistant alloy. Nussbaum et al. [] prepared (AlCrTiV)N by cathodic arc evaporation and found that with the addition of a N element, the (AlCrTiV)N HEA coating consists of TiN ceramics as well as a few Laves phases, which significantly improved the hardness and tribological performance of the coatings. Aluminum and chromium elements are widely used in those compositions for their effects on microstructure, strengthening and oxidation resistance of alloys []. Vanadium is often used to improve the frictional and wear properties because of its atomic size deforming the crystal structure of both BCC and FCC alloys []. Since the atomic radii of Al and V are much larger than those of other alloying elements, the addition of those elements will cause the atomic level stress of the HEA. In contrast, the BCC phase has a looser structure than the FCC phase. With the increase in Al content, the atomic stress of the HEA increases, which promotes the transformation of FCC structure to BCC structure, thus reducing the strain energy and Gibbs free energy []. In summary, a new equiatomic AlCrFeNiV alloy with dual-phase BCC was obtained through the combination of high-energy ball milling and a spark plasma sintering process. This strategy can be beneficial in the development of new materials that can be applied in cutting tools. The microstructure, microhardness and tribological properties were investigated in detail. The results are thus presented:(1)Microhardness reached 1076 ± 15 HV0.5, leading to a proper wear resistance. In addition, the wear behavior of AlCrFeNiV against Al2O3 ball under dry wear and lubrication conditions has been investigated. Compared with dry friction, the COF of AlCrFeNiV HEA with lubricant decreased significantly, whereas the decrease in the wear rate was not meditative.(2)The structure characterization indicates that two different kinds of body-centered cubic structures with different lattice parameters were formed in the AlCrFeNiV alloy, which is responsible for ultrahigh hardness.(3)The wear mechanism was found to be abrasive wear and oxidation wear by analyzing the worn surface.

occupying_moves.lever: Systematic variation of a minor alloying addition (e.g., 2–8 at.% Al) in the high-entropy coating
occupying_moves.technique: Magnetron sputtering for coating deposition, pin-on-disk tribometry, cross-sectional microscopy
occupying_moves.conditions: Room-temperature and elevated-temperature wear tests under controlled load and sliding speed

chosen.lever: Al doping level to tune short-range ordering
chosen.technique: Coating synthesis (magnetron sputtering), mechanical/tribological testing, microstructural analysis
chosen.conditions: Comparative pin-on-disk tests at increasing Al content under identical load and speed
chosen.why: This approach directly tests the hypothesis that short-range atomic ordering—tuned via minor element additions—governs wear behavior in high-entropy-alloy coatings. By varying the dopant fraction while keeping other parameters constant, we can observe how changes in local structure affect key properties like hardness, friction coefficient, and wear rate. If the hypothesis is correct, increased doping promoting stronger short-range order should yield measurably improved wear resistance across a range of moderate-to-high temperatures and loads. If doping variations do not alter the wear behavior as predicted, it would falsify the proposed mechanism.
